title: The Academy
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 01/12 — Introduce The Academy as a GED-focused academic RPG with a retro desktop interface. Transition: frame the learner problem as a design hypothesis, not measured research.

title: Study needs context, feedback, and a next step
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 02/12 — Present context, feedback, and a next step as a design hypothesis; state that it still needs learner validation. Transition: show the product response.

title: Study, explore, and track progress in one campus
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 03/12 — Explain how GED practice, campus exploration, and progress fit in one product. The campus details shown are illustrative. Transition: walk through a first session.

title: Create a profile, then choose a campus action
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 04/12 — Trace profile creation, starter choices, and a first study or campus action. Transition: show where those actions live.

title: A desktop shell makes the next action visible
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 05/12 — Present the retro desktop as a navigation model. The day and dashboard details are sample UI, not learner data. Transition: follow a study action through the loop.

title: Study, answer, see progress, choose again
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 06/12 — Explain the five-question set and how answers update XP, stats, and study history in the current player record. Transition: show the four subject areas.

title: One study loop covers four GED subjects
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 07/12 — Name math, language arts, science, and social studies as the four subject areas in the current practice loop. Transition: explain the mobile offline boundary.

title: Mobile study can continue offline
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 08/12 — Limit the offline claim to bundled mobile study and on-device state; do not imply web availability or cross-device sync. Transition: explain shared code without implying shared saves.

title: Web and mobile share rules, not a synced save
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 09/12 — Show shared content and game rules; make clear that web/API and mobile saves remain surface-specific. Transition: separate implemented code from future validation.

title: What exists now—and what a pilot could test
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 10/12 — Separate implemented surfaces from proposed validation and pilot steps. State there are no pilot results or learner-outcome data yet. Transition: make the pilot ask.

title: Help us test the return visit
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 11/12 — Ask for a learner or educator context, content feedback, and measures agreed in advance. This is a proposed pilot; no partner or results are claimed. Transition: close with the design goal.

title: Build a place worth returning to.
speakerNotes: CORE PATH 12/12 — Restate the design goal without promising outcomes. End the live talk here; the remaining slides are supporting material and appendix.

title: A GED study loop inside a campus world
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Use when the audience needs a high-level product summary. The app connects GED practice with campus actions and player state; do not imply synced saves.

title: A design hypothesis: make the next step visible
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Expand the design hypothesis; do not present it as learner research or a measured finding. Transition back to the product response.

title: What The Academy is
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Use for a concise product-definition detour. Describe the UI, relationship, and cross-platform components as implemented mechanisms, not proven outcomes.

title: Character choices shape the player profile
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Character traits and stats are game framing; the profile and stat board are illustrative UI. Transition to where campus actions live.

title: Assignments and quizzes make study state visible
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Treat assignment and quiz panels as illustrative UI. Show how a completed answer updates game state, not academic outcomes.

title: Progress screens summarize recorded activity
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — All displayed metrics are illustrative values, not learner results or traction. Use this slide only to explain what product state can display.

title: NPC relationships add a social layer to campus
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Dialogue and relationship examples demonstrate the design system; do not claim measured social or retention effects.

title: Dialogue can adapt to tone and relationship context
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Describe tone-aware responses as interaction logic. Do not claim they identify a learner's emotional state or improve outcomes.

title: Content packs can add themed campus events
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — The bulletin illustrates a configured theme/event pack, not a current-events feed or guaranteed weekly editorial cadence.

title: Optional AI adds descriptive texture
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — AI may enrich descriptions but does not own deterministic game state; bundled fallback text supports core behavior when enrichment is unavailable.

title: Online enrichment can add optional description detail
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Describe online generation as an optional layer with local or bundled fallback. Do not claim every surface receives identical enrichment.

title: Core study and remote enrichment use separate fallback paths
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Explain fallback behavior by surface: deterministic study content is distinct from optional remote enrichment. Do not imply every interaction is offline.

title: Illustrative day: a sequence of small decisions
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — This is an illustrative flow, not a real learner case or observed timeline. Use only when the audience needs a concrete walkthrough.

title: One study session links practice, exploration, and progress
speakerNotes: SUPPORTING — Frame the comparison as a product design lens, not a market survey or competitor claim.

title: Web, mobile, and API use a shared game boundary
speakerNotes: APPENDIX — Use for technical questions about web, mobile, and API boundaries. A shared engine does not mean shared account identity or cross-device save sync.

title: Potential contexts for a future pilot
speakerNotes: APPENDIX — These are potential future pilot contexts only; do not present any learner, educator, or partner relationship as active.

title: Core product surfaces are represented in code
speakerNotes: APPENDIX — Code presence is not traction, deployment scale, readiness, or learning evidence. Use to answer which surfaces are represented.

title: Possible partnership modes—proposed, not active
speakerNotes: APPENDIX — All partnership modes shown are proposals, not active agreements. Use only after the pilot ask or in Q&A.
